title: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, Russia says
description: At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev ha
body: At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". An oil refinery was damaged and several homes were set ablaze.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".Ukrainian officials meanwhile said eight people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Vorobyev added.Videos have emerged on social media appearing to show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged in "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election.Sunday is the third day of voting in an election that is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and which critics have dismissed as neither free, fair nor transparent.Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Sautrday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, Russia says

title: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth
description: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe
body: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too. And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters."We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son". Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent"."And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work."I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says."I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy."This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations.Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many."It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals.Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older."I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying."When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older."You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it."I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with."Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen."We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says."But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life."Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch".That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good).Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world."Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses."So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers."What does he hope young people who might catch the show will take away from it?"You don't have to have it all in place at 18, everyone is still kind of just pretending they know what they're doing."I suggest that we don't always know what we're doing in later life either.He laughs. "Exactly. Everyone's still figuring it out."Youth will debut on 21 September in the UK & Ireland on HBO Max.

schema.headline: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
description: Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets.A
body: Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets.An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported. Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized. Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass. All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. And CNN said, "we have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right".In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) - the independent, non-profit group that represents journalists who cover the US presidency - called on the administration "to immediately restore" access to the journalists and accused it of violating the First Amendment. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News.Heinrich said that the Americans, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected in their coverage "regardless of whether government officials view it favorably"."That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called Trump's White House ban illegal and unconstitutional.A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional"."The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets

title: Stephen Fleming: New England coach arrives with desire to 'beat the Aussies'
description: New Test coach Stephen Fleming said he shared English cricket's "obsession" with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to "beat the Aussies".Fleming was
body: New Test coach Stephen Fleming said he shared English cricket's "obsession" with the Ashes and arrives with the goal to "beat the Aussies".Fleming was speaking to the media for the first time since being appointed in July and ahead of taking charge for the tour of South Africa in December.Like his predecessor Brendon McCullum, Fleming is from New Zealand, the "little cousin" to Australia, in his words.The next Ashes series is in the UK next summer, when England will look to defeat the Australians for the first time since 2015 and avenge a dismal 4-1 defeat down under last winter.Asked if England are too obsessed with beating Australia, Fleming told BBC Sport: "No, because I have an obsession with it as well. New Zealand has an obsession with it, we love it."We want to beat the Aussies. We're heavily linked to England performances. We have a deep desire to beat Australia in everything, as the little cousin. We are linked, and I'm incredibly excited about being part of it."You don't think you're ever going to get that opportunity. To have that opportunity and be part of it, I can't wait."I want to be my best self and have a team that represents itself in the best possible way. I've got a vision of that and it's aspirational. It will be brilliant."Fleming, the former New Zealand captain, did not taste victory in any of the 14 Tests he played against Australia.He succeeds his former team-mate McCullum, who was sacked as Test coach earlier this summer, but remains as boss of the white-ball team. England won only two of McCullum's final 10 Tests in charge, including the hammering in Australia.Part of the criticism of England under McCullum and former captain Ben Stokes was their inability to adapt to the changing situations of Test cricket, as well as a lack of attention to detail.Fleming is a great friend of McCullum – the pair are business partners. He described the difference between the two as being: "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible."On whether a Test team should have a brand or style, Fleming said: "I don't think so. The greatest thing for a team to do is to be able to play conditions and situations."I'd love people to say we are well-planned, there's a discipline and a really strong basic structure to what we're doing, but there's also a bit of flair."The final months of McCullum's reign were dogged by late-night drinking controversies, which continued after England changed the Test coach.On Friday, Derbyshire Police announced they had closed an investigation involving England pace bowler Brydon Carse following allegations of an assault last month.Though Carse will face no action from the police, he now faces an investigation from the Cricket Regulator.He remains available for England selection, albeit has not been part of a squad in any format since the Derby incident."There are standards," said Fleming. "We pick on runs and wickets primarily, but I think it's foolish not to also say there are standards that need to be set."You need to behave in accordance with your position. We're in a very privileged position, and it's understanding that privilege and what goes along with it. It can't be convenient. You can't be when it suits you to do the right things, then when you don't want it to suit you, not."You've got to live it every day. If we can create something when you want to live it every day and better, then that's really powerful."Fleming was at Old Trafford for England's defeat of Sri Lanka in the third T20 on Saturday. Earlier in the week he visited a number of counties and met Stokes during Durham's draw against Worcestershire.Stokes abruptly retired from international cricket in July and has a previous relationship with Fleming from their time together with Chennai Super Kings at the Indian Premier League.But Fleming said he had too much "respect" for Stokes' decision to attempt to coax him out of retirement."He was in a great space, really happy, enjoying his time with Durham," said Fleming."He's got a good winter planned with the family and is very much at peace with his decision. When a player makes that decision to retire, I respect that decision 100%."To try to turn that around and question that is wrong. I know how much goes into that type of decision, and I respect that."Almost two months after being appointed Test coach, Stephen Fleming outlined what the England team may look like under his stewardship.He was calm, measured and authoritative, perhaps showing he is exactly the sort of leader England need after a chaotic period on and off the pitch.There were also signs of Fleming's character and sense of humour. He joked he has a "stress fracture of the left ear" after all the phone calls he has had with those connected with the England team, then laughed about occasionally turning up in fancy dress to relax the environment of his Chennai Super Kings team.Most revealing was the description of his relationship with Brendon McCullum – "I'll bet on the favourite and he'll bet on the longest odds possible". There were plenty of times during McCullum's reign as Test coach where those long-odds bets were placed, while Fleming seems much more likely to play the percentages.The two are great friends, which should help with a split-coaching dynamic that has not always served England well in the past. "Big brother" was one way the Fleming-McCullum dynamic was referred to, and there was a sense that England now have a grown-up in charge, following the freewheeling of McCullum.Fleming covered a range of topics: he won't try to persuade Ben Stokes to come out of retirement, he will give the World Test Championship a level of respect lacking from previous England teams, he explained he missed the Pakistan series because of family and commercial commitments.Fleming also addressed discipline and the late-night controversies that have dogged England in the past 12 months. Talk of "standards" may not be good news for Brydon Carse's prospects of a swift return to the set-up.And, of course, there was the question of "Flemball", dismissed as a "medical condition".On this evidence, Fleming's England will be more assured, mature and level than the team led by McCullum. Possibly less fun, too.The most important thing is they win more, starting in South Africa in December.

schema.headline: Stephen Fleming: New England coach arrives with desire to 'beat the Aussies'

title: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings
description: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting l
body: Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.A fresh cohort of famous faces – including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips – also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour". "Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced. Here is a list of the pairings in full: Actress Lacey Turner and Vito CoppolaReality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita KuzminHair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton and Amy DowdenAustralian singer and actress Delta Goodrem and Kai WiddringtonDJ and social media personality Cach Mercer and Maddie IngoldsbyTV and radio presenter Will Best and Dianne BuswellParalympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian CaillonActress Jaime Winstone and Carlos GuTV and stage actress Bethany Antonia and Nancy XuFormer England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis WarrPresenter and author Graeme Hall and Lauren OakleyActor Lawrence Robb and Jowita PrzystałSkeleton athlete Tabby Stoecker and Mark KarmalitaYouTuber John Nellis and Katya JonesTV and stage actress Melanie Walters and Aljaž ŠkorjanecOne pair who won't need to get to know each other are reality TV star Dani Dyer and Nikita Kuzmin.Dyer is back to compete for a second time, having withdrawn from last year's series due to a fractured ankle."I'm just over the moon. I'm so, so happy," she said after the pairing, while Kuzmin added that he had "tears of joy" in his eyes. Meanwhile, actress Bethany Antonia and professional Nancy Xu became the third two-woman couple to compete in the show. In a poignant moment, Antonia revealed that watching boxer Nicola Adams and Katya Jones performing together in Strictly's 2020 series was a "big part of my coming out journey".Among the other pairings were EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and Vito Coppola, former Paralympian Dame Sarah Storey and Julian Caillon, and Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr. Also back on the dancefloor for a final spin was reigning Strictly champion, former Lionness Karen Carney.Clad in the same diamante-encrusted football shirt, Carney recreated the Jive that first marked her out as a contender of her series, alongside dance partner Carlos Gu."I absolutely feel like I'm at home," Carney told Willis after the routine, as she paid tribute to her pro partner.  In 13 weeks' time, she'll have to surrender that glitterball trophy to a new victor.

schema.headline: Strictly is back with new hosts as celebrities discover pairings

title: Arsenal defeat at Brighton is a big lesson - Mikel Arteta
description: Since taking charge in 2019, Arteta has made a point of reiterating how much he values physicality and the demands he puts on his side to win duels. B
body: Since taking charge in 2019, Arteta has made a point of reiterating how much he values physicality and the demands he puts on his side to win duels. But against Brighton, Arsenal were dominated all over the pitch and lost challenges which they would usually be expected to win. Arteta said he was "extremely disappointed" as his side were "very far" from doing the basics he expected, with uncertainty in defence, a loss of midfield control and lack of attacking creativity.Asked why they were below par, the Spaniard added: "Well, the first one because Brighton they were really good, and they had another bite, and at the times it was better."There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50-50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them. "Sometimes there were some technical errors very much involved that opened us up in a really difficult way, but that's something to learn." He was quick to remind the media in his news conference after the game that it was still a good start to the season.The Gunners had 15 players at the World Cup which meant that a large part of the squad joined up for pre-season later than the rest of their team-mates. "That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," added Arteta. "What we've done and the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable, but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level."Brighton are currently the Premier League's top scorers with 16 goals - hitting eight of them in the past week - and could have had more against an Arsenal side who pride themselves on keeping clean sheets.The Gunners conceded the fewest goals of any side last season and just one got past David Raya in their first four league games before Saturday's defeat."It should have been more, the chances Brighton created, they were that good," said former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer on BBC Radio 5 Live."They absolutely battered Arsenal. How many times have we said that recently? From start to finish today Brighton were magnificent, every single one of them played their part."They were strong, they were fit, they went after Arsenal. They had no fear and it worked brilliantly for them, it should have been six or seven goals."The Gunners were 2-0 down at the break and have not recovered to win from such a position in a league game since March 2008 at Bolton. "Every time Brighton chased down the ball, they got it absolutely spot on. They did it as a team, they didn't do it individually," added Shearer."They thought, 'we respect Arsenal but we're not going to give them any space to play'. "The organisation was great and that just doesn't happen on it's own and you've got to give [manager] Fabian Hurzeler credit for that."Arsenal spent around £200m in the summer transfer window in a bid to strengthen the squad to challenge for more honours, and Arteta was asked if they needed reminding how tough the Premier League can be.He said: "I think they knew, I think we knew how tough it was going to be today, and the first thing that we had discussed was about the first part. "If you don't get out of that first part as winners, it will be extremely difficult to dominate the game and to have any probability of winning the game. "We knew that, but that's again credit to them for what they've done because they've overcome us and they had another edge than we did."And that's something that at this level it's extremely important to respect and to understand before anything else."Former Premier League defender Curtis Davies believed the Gunners could put the result and display down to a "blip"."Their form this season has so far been good, this has been a really shocking performance," he said on 5 Live."That defence today was nowhere near what it's used to being. The disappointment will be a set-piece goal conceded, Arsenal will have a real long look at themselves."They didn't lay a glove on Brighton, and didn't make anything of their attacking situations."

schema.headline: Arsenal defeat at Brighton is a big lesson - Mikel Arteta

title: International break: Will the three-week interlude put more pressure on managers?
description: Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results. So far this season three coaches have lost their jobs
body: Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results. So far this season three coaches have lost their jobs - Paul Heckingbottom at Preston North End, Michael Duff at Wycombe Wanderers and Peterborough's Luke Williams.But plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break.That includes the managers of Fulham and Manchester United, who on Sunday meet at Craven Cottage in the final fixture before players jet off around the world with their countries.It will all be pretty new to Alvaro Arbeloa, appointed as Fulham's manager in the summer after taking charge of just 28 games as Real Madrid boss in the second half of last season.But with no wins and three defeats in his first four Premier League matches, and speculation of unrest among the squad due to players' social media activity, the pressure is already on Arbeloa.Likewise Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, especially after the 3-2 EFL Cup exit to Brighton on Wednesday.  It was the first time United had led at home by two goals and lost since they were beaten 3-2 by Tottenham in 1976, half a century ago.Coming on the back of the 1-0 loss to 10-man Manchester City, and with their only victories this season against Ipswich Town and Sabah, Carrick needs results.But they are not the only managers who might have cause for concern.Over the past 10 years, it has been rare for a Premier League manager to be replaced this early in the campaign.Even more so in the international break.But could it be different this year? The first break is longer, three weeks rather than two, and comes later.The September slot used to come at the start of the month when clubs had only played three league fixtures. In the past 10 years only two managers - Watford's Javi Gracia in 2019 and Nottingham Forest's Nuno Espirito Santo last year - moved on during this break.What about the October stoppage? Again, only two managers have previously lost their jobs during the same period - Francesco Guidolin at Swansea in 2016, and Xisco Munoz at Watford in 2021.This suggests clubs do not tend to use an international break to change manager.It is, though, far more likely to happen in November, with six bosses replaced in the past 10 years.That does not mean managers are safe, though. The changes simply were not made during the breaks.In the past 10 campaigns, nine coaches had left their jobs by the time the second international break came along - which is where we are in the number of games.With no manager to move on yet, could it come in the next three weeks?Former Stoke, West Brom and Middlesbrough boss Tony Pulis explains when the pressure can build for a football manager.With the first international break upon us, rumblings around certain clubs that have started the season poorly have surfaced.In my time, the October/November international breaks, the pause just after the Christmas period, and then early March would be the three sticking points for any manager who was struggling with results.Why these breaks are used for clubs to make changes is plain to see. The pause in the season gives football clubs the chance to appoint a new manager with time for them to settle into their new role, to take stock of the surroundings, staff and time to prepare for their first game in charge.After Christmas, usually the first game is an FA Cup match, which again gives the new boss a chance close up to see what they have to work with. First impressions can be a vital starting point, so again the manager has time to prepare and deliver their principles to the lads.Personally, I've joined quite a few of my clubs midway through seasons, and have left a few clubs going the other way, but I do honestly believe that those international breaks, for the reasons I've given, definitely heighten the chances of struggling managers getting the sack.I don't see this September break as a flashing light, it is too early in the season, but from then on in, the dates I have mentioned really do come into play.But this early international break doesn't help any managers.Whether your team is winning or losing, on both accounts, it's a nightmare. If you're winning you want to keep playing, and yet if you've started badly as a manager you want more time to put it right. Players travelling and the chance of injuries at such an early stage of the season is completely bonkers in my opinion.While the evidence suggests things have to get pretty bad for a club to change manager early in the season, a few bosses are feeling the heat.Manchester United Simon StoneThere are ways of losing games of course, but I don't see the trip to Fulham as being 'make or break' for Carrick in the sense of his job.Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to think that way - and I agree.He got enough credit in the bank last season by steering Manchester United into the Champions League to ride out a poor start to the season.I think the issue is United generate so much debate that a loss at Craven Cottage, which would be United's first since 2009, against a team that has only one point and is bottom of the table, would lead to numerous external inquests - which in turn puts a laser focus on the club when they resume their campaign against Tottenham on 10 October.  Fulham Nizaar KinsellaIt is unclear exactly how much danger Arbeloa is in, but there appears to be some substance to reports of disgruntlement among elements of Fulham's squad early in the campaign.His significant tactical changes since replacing Marco Silva have left the Cottagers vulnerable at the back, although they produced a more solid display in a goalless draw away to Liverpool last weekend. Silva spent five years at Craven Cottage.However, owner Shahid Khan has shown a ruthless streak in the past when making managerial changes. Claudio Ranieri lasted just 106 days in charge, while Felix Magath was sacked in September 2014, albeit having been appointed the previous season.TottenhamSami MokbelThe results go from bad to worse for Tottenham. Having spent about £300m on new talent over the summer the club's owners are getting very little bang for their buck in terms of points (and goals) scored. But there is no sense whatsoever that Roberto de Zerbi is under pressure despite the club's difficult start - no wins from five games. The vibes with regards to how the team is starting to play are positive amid a sense that it is only a matter of time before they click. Of course, for Tottenham, it needs to click sooner rather than later.Crystal PalaceSami MokbelPierre Sage has endured an indifferent start to life at Palace. One league win so far hasn't gone down particularly well internally, nor has the team's leaky defence since the Frenchman's arrival from Lens. Allowances will be made for the unavailability - for a manner of reasons - of key attacking duo Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta. The 4-0 win over Lech Poznan in the Europa League on Thursday eased some of the pressure, but a defeat at Leeds this afternoon would come at the worst possible time for Sage.BurnleyNicky Hayen quit Genk to spearhead Burnley's bid to return to the Premier League at the first attempt.The Clarets started the season as third favourites for promotion, behind West Ham and Wolves, but are winless in their first eight matches.In his pre-match news conference on Friday, the Belgian faced questions about his future.Hayen admitted he was under pressure and Saturday's game against fellow slow starters Derby was a must-win fixture.But a disappointing 1-1 draw, with the Rams scoring a stoppage-time leveller, left Burnley rock-bottom going into the break.The Burnley board might now be assessing their options. Derby manager John Eustace, who almost took the club to the play-offs last season, is not safe either with the club in the relegation zone.WatfordA Watford manager can never rest easy in their seat. Alessio Dionisi, appointed in the summer, became their 27th permanent manager in just under 18 years.Friday's defeat at Bristol City left the Hornets with two wins from their first eight league games under the Italian, who managed Empoli before moving to England.Sitting in 19th position in the league table, three points above the drop zone, it would not be a surprise if owner Gino Pozzo decided to make an early change.

schema.headline: International break: Will the three-week interlude put more pressure on managers?

title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles
description: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on
body: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.Saudi authorities said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh on Saturday, without confirming any further strikes or causalities. Earlier, a column of black smoke was seen rising from fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport, where flights were disrupted temporarily on Saturday. Air raid alerts had sounded in the capital for the first time since the Iran-backed Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia in July.The US state department urged Americans in the Middle East to "exercise vigilance and be prepared for potential flight cancellations and other travel disruptions"."Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," it said in a statement. It added that Americans "should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region".Air defences also stopped "hostile attempts to target civilians" in the cities of Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu, an official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.  He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which is currently controlled by the Houthis.Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.      On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external.A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations., externalAn AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts."I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.      On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

schema.headline: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles

title: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' at first show since Macklemore controversy in Philadelphia
description: Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes" as he opened his first show since Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestin
body: Ed Sheeran has apologised to fans for making "mistakes" as he opened his first show since Macklemore was dropped from his tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.The singer began his concert in Philadelphia by addressing the controversy that has since engulfed the tour and prompted all of his support acts to quit."I never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran said.He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific" and called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable".The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him. The row has seen ticket prices drop and sales decline for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour.Sheeran told the crowd that while he was used to facing criticism for his music, "this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry".He said he wanted to "address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand". "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division", he continued. "But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore."Sheeran said what happened in Israel on 7 October was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain", and what was happening in Gaza was "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate". "My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."He said he was working out how to contribute in a way that would help "victims of these terrible times - and listening and learning, because I do not know enough".Some protesters waved flags outside the venue, but the concert proceeded largely unfettered.A protester who gave his name as Cooper said he had come out "to support the struggle for" the Palestinian people."We need more people like Macklemore and other artists who have a voice, who have a public platform, to be able to speak on behalf of the Palestinian people and their struggle for liberation, especially in the United States," he said.Of the handful of ticket-holders who stopped to talk to the BBC prior to the show, there was a sentiment of determination to enjoy an evening of music while at the same time supporting freedom of speech.Reacting to Sheeran's remarks as they later left the venue, one fan said he had "covered both sides nicely, and I think everyone leaves happy", while another called his speech "very sincere, and I think that's what the people wanted to hear was sincerity".The controversy began in early September, when Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters and referred to the death toll in Gaza as a genocide, a claim Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters".Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such Gillette Stadium in Boston, Massachusetts - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed.Billionaire Robert Kraft who owns Gillette Stadium and the American football team the New England Patriots, confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows.Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said he was "only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas".Meanwhile, support acts including Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish musician Lukas Graham and his backing band Beoga quit the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.The artists argued his removal represented a chilling effect on free speech.Do you have tickets? Get in touch by using this link or the form below.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' at first show since Macklemore controversy in Philadelphia

title: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity
description: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisatio
body: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation."It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says."In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages."Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says."I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people."It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world.There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between.In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership.The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong.After 43 years together, Min, 77, and his late partner Tim, had discussed their plans for a future where one of them would live alone, as Tim's health deteriorated.While schemes like Kindred House and Tonic are welcomed by Mindy, Norman and Min, the Spotlight on Ageing report warns that, because the older LGBTQ+ population is growing, the demand for specialist services is expected to outstrip supply.Between 2019 and 2024, the number of over-50s identifying as lesbian, gay or bisexual in the UK increased by around a third - from roughly 340,000 to almost 460,000.There was a 4% rise in the number of heterosexual people aged 50 and above in the same period.These numbers are projected to continue to increase as the relatively larger younger generations of people identifying as LGBTQ+ age.Porter warns that without more schemes like Kindred House, and more training and awareness for those in other care settings, the ageing population may struggle to get proper support.For Mindy, who is part of a steering group advising on the plans, knowing there may be more options available in the future is reassuring."It's important that you can go, that you think, 'You know what, I could live there because I know the staffing, the ethics, the rules, everything about the place has been put together from an LGBTQ+ focus,'" she says."That's what we've been doing and it's something I'm really proud of being a part of."

schema.headline: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity

title: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana
description: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duches
body: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face."If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied."And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example."I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan. He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness". His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly-worded response to his claims about King Charles.That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life."I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

schema.headline: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana

title: Maddy Cusack: Remember the person, not just the player, family says
description: Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fu
body: Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming"."It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat."They're very difficult days."Olivia and Emily often come to Maddy's memorial bench in Scargill Park in West Hallam, Derbyshire, which is where they all grew up. With both of their birthdays at the end of October, Emily says they'd always planned to spend them together, but "now I just come here"."She used to get us in trouble with my dad when we were younger," she says. "It was always her idea then I'd take the blame for it."In an inquest focusing on darker times in her life, it's this side of Maddy that her family thinks has got lost. Olivia, along with other members of Maddy's family, has campaigned tirelessly since her sister's death, setting up a foundation in her name to support aspiring female footballers. "The foundation keeps me going," she says. "It's been a real lifeline to be able to continue her story."On Saturday, she organised a walk from Bramall Lane, Sheffield United's ground, to near Derby where Maddy lived - a distance of almost 30 miles."The aim with the walk is just to do her proud," Olivia says. "Maddy would love that we were all challenging ourselves."

schema.headline: Maddy Cusack: Remember the person, not just the player, family says

title: Meta glasses: Is it okay to film people in public places?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered withByOlivia Copela
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered withByOlivia CopelandBBC News NIIt's the latest wearable tech boom that is likely coming to a street, park or town square near you. But not everyone sees the future of smart glasses as rose-tinted.The technology allows users to make calls, interact with AI hands-free and also take photos and videos simply by touching the frames, provoking concerns about privacy.Wetherspoons, which runs almost 800 pubs across the UK, has banned using the glasses to film inside its premises and women's rights campaigners have raised issues about their potential use for harassment.But, with videos from content creators continuing to thrive on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, the debate of how to best use the glasses in public places will continue to go back and forth.Pearse Vallely is one of those content creators – the 31-year-old from Ballymurphy, in west Belfast, makes a living from his work on social media.He uses a pair of Meta Ray-Ban glasses, with most of his videos showing his glasses-eye view of walking down the street as he greets passers-by with rhyming phrases.One of his most popular videos, filmed in Belfast city centre, hit 600,000 views on TikTok.Image source, Pearse VallelyImage caption, Content creator Pearse Vallely, wearing his Meta glasses, said he uses them "in a positive way"The success of the videos rely on their good-natured vibe. He said he had never posted a video after being asked not to, and no one had ever got in touch to ask him to take down a video."I think it's because of the nature of my conversation with them. They know I'm not making an eejit out of them, I'm doing it in a positive way."Meta glasses, the brand used by Vallely, are the market leader in the smart glasses boom, with the company saying more than seven million pairs have been sold to date.This TikTok post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on TikTokThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. TikTok content may contain adverts.Skip tiktok video by Pearsey-WearseyAllow TikTok content?This article contains content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read TikTok’s cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. TikTok content may contain adverts.Available for a few hundred pounds, and made in partnership with the firm behind famed sunglasses brand Ray-Bans, the frames feature an unobtrusive camera that users can activate via touch.This turns on a pulsing white light, which aims to let people know when a video is being taken, and a flash for photos – a feature a Meta spokesperson said "smartphones and other cameras don't have".Meta said it recently updated the glasses to disable the camera if the light was tampered with.Should AI or smart glasses products from more companies end up selling as well as Meta's version, researchers expect as many as 100 million people will buy a pair in the next few years.Valelly, whose videos rely on the interactions being spontaneous and natural, said people are often aware he is recording due to the light on his glasses.He also said he tries to let people know he has recorded them after filming if he can catch them in time.In Northern Ireland, it is generally legal to film someone even discreetly in a public place, as people in public do not usually have a reasonable expectation of privacy.The filming would only be unlawful if it could be seen as harassment, stalking, if the footage is voyeuristic, or in circumstances where there would be a reasonable expectation of privacy.Image caption, The smart glasses can be used to make calls hands-free, play music in ear and take photos and videos"It's okay to have a 30-second conversation with someone," Vallely said."I think that's something we're losing due to technology, and I'm trying to use technology to spin it around."Vallely said he could understand the reasoning behind banning wearing Meta glasses "if people are being crude and rude", but he said the intention behind filming was key."People know it's me doing it, while other people do it on troll accounts. No matter what is invented, people are going to use things for the wrong reasons."Still, while Vallely said he hasn't run into any opposition, there are reports suggesting an increased friction between people using the glasses to film and the general public.Last December, people hailed a woman as "a hero" after she snapped a man's Meta glasses in two on the New York subway. In July, police in Scotland began an investigation after complaints over a TikToker who used the glasses to secret film members of the public.Referring to the company's ban on filming, a Wetherspoons spokesperson said smart glasses breached "common sense by enabling surreptitious surveillance" while Monopoly Events, which runs Comic Con Northern Ireland, also banned wearing the glasses at its events over concerns about secret recording.Meanwhile, TikTok videos of users approaching women, asking for their number and filming their reaction to pick-up lines, are often posted with the hashtag #howtogetagirlfriend and can garner thousands of views.Harassment concernsImage caption, Women's rights campaigners say the glasses pose risks to privacyElaine Crory, a women's sector lobbyist at the Women's Resource and Development Agency, said there's a lack of awareness about when and how the glasses are being used, leading to issues around consent."Right now, if you're filming with a camera or with your phone, I usually can see that and then avoid that. But you may not be aware you're being filmed with an AI camera."She added there were also concerns the glasses were being used for things that are currently illegal, like upskirting.Crory said people can appeal to social media sites to take videos down and some venues have put up signs "on a case by case basis", but she feels legislation has not caught up with the technology."A person has no legal redress if they are filmed in the street, on a bus, in a classroom," she said.The Department of Justice (DoJ) said that while the regulation of Meta glasses was not a DoJ specific matter, if the use of the glasses involved "behaviour that crosses the criminal threshold, then existing offences such as 'up-skirting' as a form of voyeurism" were available.Image caption, Optometrist Geoff McConville says the glasses are "ground-breaking" for visually-impaired usersFor optometrist Geoff McConville, who stocks Meta glasses in his Belfast shop, there are concerns about their "inappropriate use", but there are also beneficial aspects to the technology.He cites how his patients use text-to-speech features, allowing them to read newspapers and signs with AI."For my elderly, visually impaired patients, they are ground-breaking. They are amazing."In a statement, Meta said the glasses provided "critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards"."Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently."In a recent Q&A session, the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said if people posted content "taking advantage of people and harassing them... then we're going to take the content down".

schema.headline: Meta glasses: Is it okay to film people in public places?

title: Oldham Asian hornet hunt leads to nest discovery
description: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Food traps were used to attract the hornets before monitoring the direction and timing of their flightsByMichelle
body: Image source, HandoutImage caption, Food traps were used to attract the hornets before monitoring the direction and timing of their flightsByMichelle AdamsonReporting fromin Oldham and Naj ModakNorth WestBeekeepers who feared a damaging new arrival of Asian hornets in the Greater Manchester area helped track down their nest after sightings sparked an urgent search.The nest of the non-native invasive insects, which prey on honey bees and threatens biodiversity, was found in Oldham, after local keepers worked with government bee inspectors to trace them using GPS trackers and food traps.The Asian hornets were first spotted three weeks ago in Oldham, prompting concerns the species may be spreading further north.Beekeeper, Cath Charnock, said: "We weren't expecting to see any this soon in our area."Image caption, Local beekeepers Cath Charnock and Les Latham worked alongside government bee inspectors to trace the insectsCharnock said two credible sightings were received within a short period, which prompted them to take action.Fellow beekeeper Les Latham said the team used food traps to attract the insects before monitoring the direction and timing of their flights.By repeating the process at different locations, they were able to build up a picture of where the nest was likely to be.Government bee inspectors then joined the search, using GPS radio trackers and AI-assisted cameras to narrow down the location.Image source, HandoutImage caption, A single nest could consume about 15kg (two stone) of insects in one seasonLatham said several search teams eventually converged on the same spot before inspectors used binoculars to identify the nest in a tree.A single nest could consume about 15kg (two stone) of insects in one season, affecting not only honeybees but also hoverflies, moths, spiders, wasps and other species, she said.Charnock urged the public to report suspected sightings using the Asian Hornet Watch app, calling on people to "see it, snap it and app it".Asian hornets pose no greater threat to humans than native hornets, and if you get stung by one, the advice is to immediately wash the area with cold water and soap, then apply ice to stop the venom spreading further.But the main prey of the Asian hornet is honeybees, with one insect killing up to 50 bees a day, devastating entire colonies.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

schema.headline: Oldham Asian hornet hunt leads to nest discovery

title: Twin's stillbirth inspires grieving Stratford father's children's book
description: Warning: This story covers stillbirths and some people may find the details distressingOne date is etched into Richard Ganjavi's memory: 6 August 2024
body: Warning: This story covers stillbirths and some people may find the details distressingOne date is etched into Richard Ganjavi's memory: 6 August 2024. It was the day for the routine 34-week scan for the twins he was expecting with his wife, Naomi."The room went quiet. [The woman doing the scan] said the words that shattered everything: "I'm so sorry, there isn't a heartbeat."Naomi and Richard were rushed from Stratford Hospital to Warwick Hospital but Bella was stillborn."We just fell to pieces," Richard said.In the time since then, Bella's twin sister, Penny, who was born healthily, has just celebrated her second birthday. In those two years, Richard said he processed his grief by writing a children's book, Whispers of a Purple Butterfly, inspired by his story.The primary school teacher started writing within weeks of the loss of Bella."We had two cots upstairs, two seats in the car, a double pram. Two years on we could be walking down the street, and see someone with twins and every time it just gets you," he admitted."In a way you never get over it."The book is about Lucy, a fictional 10-year-old who is the surviving twin of a similar situation and aimed at eight to 12 year olds.Richard, who lives in Meon Vale, near Stratford-upon-Avon, said the process was "a way of getting it down and out of my head".But  the novel has since taken on a larger meaning for the family with Richard reading it to Penny, so she has something when she is old enough to understand, "to know that she will always be enough".The reaction from those who have read the book had blown Richard away, he admitted."I've had so many messages from bereaved parents, people who've lost a family member or a close friend," he said."They've all said, after reading the book, 'wow, where was it when I needed it'."He hoped charities, teachers and therapists could use the book to help those dealing with the loss of a baby.Richard and Naomi make regular visits to the hospital's Rainbow Garden, where Bella has a glass leaf in her memory.They have become friends with nurses and midwives at the special care baby unit who looked after Penny as well as them, after the loss of Bella.Two of the midwives went on to become Penny's godmothers."We've really built a relationship with Richard and Naomi, and it's really lovely to see them coming back," Lead nurse Bettina Powell said."It's really important...to remember the loss of Bella.""It's been so lovely watching Penny grow, seeing how they navigate everything and all the things they've done," neonatal nurse Teri added."It's been so lovely feeling part of their journey."Richard said he wanted his book be become a lasting legacy for Bella"We are so proud of Penny but we're also proud of Bella. When we talk about her, we say her name with pride," he said."The grief doesn't go away, but the world around our grief has got bigger."If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Twin's stillbirth inspires grieving Stratford father's children's book
